personas.description: Consultants who design data-first marketing solutions on Data 360 and advise clients on Marketing Cloud Next architecture and implementation.

personas.label: Marketing Cloud Engagement practitioners moving to Next

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Marketing Cloud Next Consultant Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam tests whether you can design data-first marketing solutions on Data 360, orchestrate AI-driven campaigns through Agentforce and Flow, and advise on Marketing Cloud Next architecture, not just operate the send tool.
bullets: 60 scored questions plus up to five unscored questions that do not affect your result.
Exam fee: US$200; retake fee: US$100, plus applicable taxes.
No formal prerequisite, but hands-on Marketing Cloud Next implementation or administration experience is strongly recommended.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Book the exam once you can explain data modeling and segmentation on Data 360, consent management, journey design, and sending-domain setup for Marketing Cloud Next without defaulting to classic Marketing Cloud Engagement answers.

examFormat.heading: Marketing Cloud Next Consultant Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is a proctored, scenario-based multiple-choice and multiple-select test delivered online or at a test center.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Expect scenario-based questions about setup and governance, data modeling and segmentation, journey design, sending domains and consent, and reporting on Marketing Cloud Next.
bestWayToPass: Know setup and governance: org-level configuration, roles, and governance decisions specific to Marketing Cloud Next.
Master data modeling and segmentation: how Data 360 models customer data and how segments are built from it for targeting.
Understand consent management: how consent signals gate which channels and journeys a contact can receive.
Design journeys with Agentforce and Flow: know how AI-orchestrated campaign steps fit alongside traditional Flow-based journey logic.

expertInsight: Use Salesforce's official Marketing Cloud Next Consultant exam guide and the Trailhead prep trail (roughly 5,500 points) as the study scope. This is a newly launched 2026 credential built on Data Cloud, so don't assume classic Marketing Cloud Engagement study material covers the Data 360 data model, consent, or Agentforce-orchestration topics correctly.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests your ability to design data-first marketing solutions on Data 360, orchestrate AI campaigns via Agentforce and Flow, and advise on Marketing Cloud Next architecture and implementation. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 72% pass mark.
topics: Journey Design with Agentforce and Flow

keyConcepts.h2: Marketing Cloud Next Consultant: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Setup and Governance
blocks.body: Marketing Cloud Next is built directly on Data 360, so initial setup decisions (business unit structure, user roles, governance of who can build segments and journeys) have a bigger architectural impact than in classic Marketing Cloud Engagement, where data and sends lived in a more self-contained environment.

blocks.heading: Data Modeling and Segmentation
blocks.body: Segments are built against the unified Data 360 customer profile rather than a Marketing Cloud-only data extension. Consultants need to know how source data maps into that model and how segment logic reads from it.

blocks.heading: Consent Management
blocks.body: Consent signals captured in Data 360 gate which channels and journeys a given contact is eligible for. A journey design that ignores current consent state, or relies on stale consent data, is a compliance and deliverability risk.

blocks.heading: Journey Design with Agentforce and Flow
blocks.body: Marketing Cloud Next lets Agentforce agents orchestrate parts of a campaign (such as content selection or send timing) alongside explicit Flow logic. Consultants should know where AI orchestration is appropriate versus where a deterministic Flow step is required.

blocks.heading: Sending Domains and Deliverability
blocks.body: Sending domain configuration (authentication, reputation, and domain setup) still determines inbox placement on Marketing Cloud Next, the same way it did on classic Marketing Cloud Engagement, even though the campaign orchestration layer has changed.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Marketing Cloud Next Consultant Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions describe a client marketing scenario and ask you to choose the Data 360-native configuration, not the classic Marketing Cloud Engagement equivalent.

blocks.heading: Default to Data 360, not Data Extensions
blocks.body: If an answer choice describes a classic Marketing Cloud Engagement Data Extension pattern where a Data 360-native segment or calculated insight would apply instead, that classic-pattern answer is usually the trap.

blocks.heading: Trace consent before trace content
blocks.body: When a scenario asks why a contact didn't receive a message, check consent and eligibility signals before assuming it's a content or send-time issue.

blocks.heading: Know when Agentforce orchestration is the better fit
blocks.body: Agentforce fits well for adaptive, judgment-based steps (like picking the best-performing content variant); a strictly sequential, rules-based step is usually still a Flow concern.

blocks.heading: Separate deliverability from targeting
blocks.body: A low open rate is often a sending-domain/deliverability issue; a low relevant-audience size is a segmentation issue. Don't conflate the two when picking a fix.

blocks.heading: Watch for Omni-Channel and Service Cloud crossover
blocks.body: Some scenarios blend into Service Cloud or Omni-Channel considerations when a journey hands off to service; know the boundary between marketing orchestration and service-side execution.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Consultant Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this credential, round out your marketing and data consultant track:

sampleQuestions.question: A client asks why Marketing Cloud Next segments behave differently from the Data Extensions they used in classic Marketing Cloud Engagement. What is the core architectural reason?
options: Segments are stored in a spreadsheet instead of a database
Segments are built against the unified Data 360 customer profile rather than a Marketing-Cloud-only data store
Segments can no longer be filtered by any criteria
Segments require a separate paid add-on to function at all
sampleQuestions.explanation: Marketing Cloud Next segmentation reads from the unified Data 360 profile, which is why it behaves differently from a self-contained Data Extension model.
whyWrong: Marketing Cloud Next data is managed through Data 360, not spreadsheets.
Segments can still be filtered with logic; the architecture change is about the underlying data source, not filtering capability.
Segmentation is core functionality, not a separate paid add-on.

sampleQuestions.question: A contact withdraws email consent, but a scheduled journey still shows them as eligible for tomorrow's send. What should the consultant check first?
options: The email subject line length
Whether the journey's eligibility check reads current consent state from Data 360 before sending
The sender's email signature
The number of images in the email template
sampleQuestions.explanation: If a contact who withdrew consent is still shown as eligible, the journey's eligibility logic likely isn't re-checking current consent state before the send.
whyWrong: Subject line length has no bearing on consent eligibility.
An email signature is a content detail, unrelated to consent-based eligibility.
Image count is a content/design detail, unrelated to whether a send should be gated by consent.

sampleQuestions.question: A client wants an AI-driven step that picks the best-performing content variant for each contact in real time. Which approach fits best?
options: A strictly sequential Flow with no decision logic
An Agentforce-orchestrated step that adapts content selection based on performance signals
A manually updated spreadsheet of content choices
Disabling personalization entirely
sampleQuestions.explanation: Adaptive, judgment-based content selection is exactly the kind of step Agentforce orchestration is designed for within Marketing Cloud Next journeys.
whyWrong: A strictly sequential Flow with no decision logic can't adapt content choice based on performance, which is what's required here.
A manual spreadsheet can't operate in real time at scale for every contact.
Disabling personalization contradicts the stated goal of picking the best-performing variant per contact.

sampleQuestions.question: Email open rates have dropped sharply even though the audience size and content are unchanged. What should the consultant investigate first?
options: The segmentation logic
Sending domain authentication and reputation
The journey's entry criteria
The content's font choice
sampleQuestions.explanation: A sharp, unexplained open-rate drop with stable audience and content points to a deliverability issue, most often sending domain authentication or reputation.
whyWrong: Segmentation logic affects who is targeted, not the inbox-placement problem described here where the audience is unchanged.
Entry criteria determine who enters the journey, not a deliverability drop given a stable audience.
Font choice is a cosmetic detail, not a cause of an open-rate collapse.

sampleQuestions.question: A journey step hands a contact off to a live service conversation after they click a specific link. Which capability is primarily responsible for that handoff?
options: A Marketing Cloud Next sending domain
Omni-Channel routing on the service side receiving the handoff
A Data 360 segment definition
A consent management policy
sampleQuestions.explanation: Handing a contact from a marketing journey into a live conversation is a service-side routing concern, typically handled by Omni-Channel.
whyWrong: Sending domain configuration affects deliverability, not conversation routing.
A segment definition controls targeting, not live conversation handoff.
Consent policy gates eligibility for communications, not how a live handoff is routed.

sampleQuestions.question: Which statement best describes governance considerations when setting up Marketing Cloud Next for a large enterprise client?
options: Governance only matters for small clients
Business unit structure and role-based access to segments and journeys should reflect the org's real marketing team boundaries
Every marketer should have unrestricted access to every segment
Governance settings cannot be changed after initial setup
sampleQuestions.explanation: Because Marketing Cloud Next governance decisions have a bigger architectural footprint on a Data 360-native platform, they should map to the client's real team and data-access boundaries.
whyWrong: Governance matters at any scale, but is especially important for large, multi-team enterprise clients.
Unrestricted universal access defeats the purpose of role-based governance.
Governance settings can generally be adjusted as the org evolves, they aren't fixed forever at initial setup.

sampleQuestions.question: A consultant needs to combine purchase history, support case data, and web behavior into one profile to drive a segment. Where does this unification happen in Marketing Cloud Next?
options: Inside a single Marketing Cloud Engagement Data Extension
In the Data 360 unified customer profile that Marketing Cloud Next reads from
In a separate Excel workbook maintained manually
It cannot be done; each data source must stay separate
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data 360 is the unification layer that combines data from multiple sources into one customer profile that Marketing Cloud Next can segment against.
whyWrong: A single Data Extension reflects the classic Marketing Cloud Engagement pattern, not the Data 360-native approach.
Manual spreadsheet unification doesn't scale and isn't how the platform is designed to unify data.
Unifying multi-source data for segmentation is exactly what Data 360 is built to do.

sampleQuestions.question: A journey needs to pause a contact until a specific consent type is granted, then resume. What is the correct design approach?
options: Send the message regardless of consent and apologize later if needed
Add a wait/decision step that checks current consent state before allowing the contact to proceed
Remove the contact from the journey permanently
Ignore consent since the client approved the campaign
sampleQuestions.explanation: A wait/decision step that re-checks consent state is the correct way to gate progression on a consent requirement that may change over time.
whyWrong: Sending regardless of consent status creates compliance risk and defeats the purpose of consent management.
Permanently removing the contact doesn't allow them to proceed once they do grant consent later.
Client campaign approval does not override an individual contact's consent status.

sampleQuestions.question: Which factor is most directly responsible for inbox placement (not landing in spam) for a Marketing Cloud Next send?
options: The journey's entry segment size
Sending domain authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC-style setup) and sender reputation
The number of personalization tokens used
The journey's internal name
sampleQuestions.explanation: Domain authentication and sender reputation are the primary technical levers for inbox placement, independent of audience size or internal naming.
whyWrong: Segment size affects how many people are targeted, not whether the message reaches the inbox versus spam.
Personalization token count is a content detail, not a deliverability authentication factor.
A journey's internal name has no effect on mailbox provider filtering decisions.

sampleQuestions.question: A client's compliance team wants a report showing exactly which contacts received which consent-gated message and when. What should the consultant recommend?
options: Rely on each marketer's personal notes
Build reporting against journey send and consent-check history captured in the platform
Estimate the numbers at the end of each quarter
Tell the compliance team this cannot be tracked
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform-captured send and consent-check history gives an auditable, accurate basis for compliance reporting, rather than informal or estimated tracking.
whyWrong: Personal notes are not an auditable or reliable compliance record.
Estimating figures doesn't meet a compliance team's need for exact send/consent records.
This kind of send and consent history is trackable within the platform, so dismissing it as impossible is incorrect.

sampleQuestions.question: A marketer wants to reuse the same journey logic across two business units with different sending domains. What is the best practice?
options: Hard-code one business unit's domain into the shared journey
Parameterize the sending configuration so each business unit's journey instance uses its own domain
Duplicate the entire Data 360 profile for each business unit
Disable sending domains for both business units
sampleQuestions.explanation: Parameterizing sending configuration per business unit lets shared journey logic be reused correctly without one unit's sends going out under the wrong domain.
whyWrong: Hard-coding one business unit's domain breaks correct sending for the other business unit.
Duplicating the entire unified profile per business unit defeats the purpose of a single unified Data 360 model.
Disabling sending domains entirely would break deliverability authentication for both business units.

sampleQuestions.question: A consultant is asked whether Agentforce can fully replace Flow for journey orchestration on a compliance-sensitive campaign. What is the most accurate answer?
options: Yes, Agentforce should always fully replace Flow
No, deterministic, rules-based compliance steps are generally still better suited to explicit Flow logic
No, Agentforce cannot be used in any journey
Yes, but only on weekends
sampleQuestions.explanation: Agentforce fits adaptive, judgment-based steps well, but deterministic compliance-critical logic is generally better served by explicit, auditable Flow steps.
whyWrong: Treating Agentforce as a full replacement for all orchestration ignores where deterministic logic is actually required.
Agentforce can be used within journeys; it isn't categorically excluded.
There's no day-of-week restriction on how orchestration tools can be used.

sampleQuestions.question: A segment built on Data 360 returns far fewer contacts than expected. What should the consultant check first?
options: The email template's color scheme
Whether the underlying source data was correctly mapped and unified into the profile the segment reads from
The journey's send time
The marketer's job title
sampleQuestions.explanation: An unexpectedly small segment usually traces back to a data mapping/unification issue in the profile the segment is built against, not a cosmetic or scheduling detail.
whyWrong: Color scheme is a content detail with no effect on how many contacts match a segment definition.
Send time affects when a journey fires, not how many contacts a segment matches.
A marketer's job title has no bearing on segment match counts.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes the relationship between Marketing Cloud Next and Marketing Cloud Engagement for an existing client?
options: They are the exact same product with a different name
Marketing Cloud Next is a separate, Data Cloud-native platform; migrating from Engagement requires rethinking data, segmentation, and journey design
Marketing Cloud Engagement customers are automatically and silently moved to Next with no changes
Marketing Cloud Next only supports SMS, not email
sampleQuestions.explanation: Marketing Cloud Next is architecturally distinct, built on Data Cloud/Data 360, so moving from Engagement involves real redesign of data, segmentation, and journeys, not a simple rename.
whyWrong: They share a brand family but are architecturally distinct products, not the same system under a new name.
Migration is a deliberate implementation project, not a silent automatic move with zero changes.
Marketing Cloud Next supports email and other channels, it is not SMS-only.

sampleQuestions.question: A client asks how Agentforce decides which content variant to show a given contact in a journey step. What should the consultant explain?
options: It is chosen entirely at random with no data input
It uses performance signals and the contact's unified profile data to select the most relevant variant
It always picks the most recently created variant regardless of performance
It requires the marketer to manually pick a variant for every single contact
sampleQuestions.explanation: Agentforce orchestration uses performance data and the contact's profile to adaptively select content, which is the value proposition over manual or random selection.
whyWrong: Random selection with no data input would defeat the purpose of AI-driven personalization.
Always picking the newest variant ignores performance data entirely, which isn't how adaptive selection works.
Requiring manual per-contact selection at scale is exactly what AI orchestration is meant to avoid.
